idiom_name: package per module; internal for build-module privacy, top-level private for file scope
implementation_notes: Kotlin packages are namespaces only - they need not match folders and carry no access semantics - so the module's encapsulation comes from the visibility model: top-level declarations are public by default, internal makes them visible anywhere in the same compilation module (a Gradle source set, a Maven project or an IDE module), and a top-level private declaration is file-scoped. A domain module is therefore a package whose published surface is its public top-level declarations, with everything else marked internal or private. Because internal spans the build module rather than the package, package-level privacy must be expressed by keeping helpers file-private or by splitting the build module; on the JVM internal members become public in bytecode with mangled names, so the boundary is compiler-checked for Kotlin callers but not for Java clients.
pitfalls: internal is module-wide, not package-wide, so two packages in the same Gradle module share their internals - the module is only as fine-grained as the build module.
internal becomes public in JVM bytecode (with name mangling), so Java and reflective code can still reach internals; do not treat it as a security boundary.
Packages are orthogonal to directories, so file layout and the model drift apart silently unless the folder convention is enforced by review or tooling.
